# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Review: Varga & Holm, Comment on the Halden Pilot

The comment does useful work with the microdata. Its most important finding is that 7 of the 9 withdrawals happened *after* the reduced schedule began, mostly for workload reasons. That contradicts the working paper's own description of the withdrawals and should be corrected on the record. The comparison of manager-reported and record-based output is also valuable. A gap in 19 of 23 organisations would be very unlikely by chance (sign test p ≈ 0.003, two-sided), so the overstatement looks systematic. Several of the problems it documents (attrition, scheduled hours, nominal revenue) are among those I flagged in the working paper earlier.

The main problems are that the conclusion goes well beyond the evidence, one of the three corrections claimed in the abstract is never made, and the comment applies stricter standards to evidence it disputes than to its own.

## Arithmetic

Most figures reproduce:
- 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859, a fall of 14.1%.
- 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861, a fall of 13.9%.
- 95.4 / 0.861 = 1.108, a gain of 10.8%.
- All four rows of Table 2 reproduce.
- Real revenue: 1.014 / 1.041 = 0.974, a fall of 2.6%.

Two figures don't reproduce:

- **The hours decomposition doesn't add up.** Four days at +0.7 hours each gives 2.8 hours. Adding 1.6 hours on the day off gives 4.4 hours above the 32 scheduled, so about 36.4 hours. The reported actual is 34.6. If the 1.6-hour figure is right, the four-day figure must be about +0.25 hours per day, not +0.7. The authors should check which figure is wrong or explain what the two averages are averaged over.
- **The energy extrapolation reaches zero at about month 9, not "around month ten."** The decline is 0.32 SD over three months. At that rate, the remaining 0.29 SD runs out about 2.7 months after month six, at roughly month 8.7.

## 1. The conclusion contradicts the comment's own evidence

The abstract says the four problems "account for most of the reported gain." The conclusion says the gains are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty." These claims are inconsistent, and the stronger one isn't supported.

- **There is a residual gain the comment doesn't explain.** After the corrections, +10.8% remains. Attributing it to novelty is a hypothesis, and the comment never tests it (see §4).
- **The comment ignores the Varden result that contradicts it.** It calls Varden's counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature," but doesn't mention Varden's case-processing stratum from the same trial. That stratum found +12.5% output per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4). It had randomisation, administrative output and timesheet hours, so measurement and selection can't explain it. Only novelty remains as a possible explanation over nine months, and the comment offers no evidence for that. Citing one stratum of a trial as the most reliable evidence while omitting the other stratum is selective.

A defensible conclusion would be roughly: corrections roughly halve the reported gain in the subset where they can be made; the residual may be partly novelty; randomised evidence suggests real per-hour gains in backlog work but not in coverage-bound work.

## 2. The headline correction isn't what the abstract says it is

- **Attrition is never corrected.** The abstract says "Correcting the first three, the gain … falls from 23.4% to 10.8%." The first three problems include attrition. But no row of Table 2 adjusts for the withdrawn organisations; the 17 organisations in the final row are all survivors. The comment documents attrition well but doesn't correct for it. If output data exist for the withdrawals, impute them or report bounds. If no data exist, at least show what the result would be under assumed outcomes, such as an output index of 80–90 for the withdrawals.
- **23.4% → 10.8% compares different samples.** The 23.4% is for all 61 organisations. The 10.8% is for 17 organisations that are not a random subset, as the Data Note itself concedes. Part of the drop could reflect who is in the subset rather than the corrections. Report the as-reported figure for the same 17 organisations (manager index ÷ 0.8) so the effect of the corrections is shown like-for-like. The Data Note's caveat belongs in the abstract too.

## 3. The record-based output measure needs scrutiny

The comment treats records as the truth, but one of the record types is "billable hours delivered." In professional services, billable hours fall almost mechanically when working time falls. Using billable hours as output and then dividing by hours partly measures the billable share of time, not productivity. The comment should:
- show how many of the 23 (and of the 17) used billable hours;
- report the comparison with and without them.

The manager index may also capture things records miss, such as project work and quality. The 19-of-23 pattern still suggests upward bias, but some of the 3.8-point gap may come from differences in coverage rather than rounding toward success.

## 4. The novelty argument doesn't use the direct evidence available

- **A survey proxy stands in for output.** The novelty claim rests on two self-reported energy readings, extrapolated linearly. Energy is not output, and two points can't distinguish a decline toward zero from a plateau.
- **The comment could test this directly.** The Halden output index was collected *monthly*. The microdata should show whether output per hour declined from month to month during the pilot. If it did, that is real evidence for novelty. If it didn't, the argument is weakened.
- **"The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter"** is rhetoric, not analysis. A six-month study can't establish durability, but it also can't establish novelty.

## 5. The treatment of the Varden meetings analysis is inaccurate and uneven

- **"Fitted to a subgroup" is wrong.** The seven treated case-processing offices are a pre-registered randomisation stratum, not a subgroup selected afterward.
- **"Selected for analysis after the results were known" is also wrong.** Varden says the meeting data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results.
- **Varden already gave these caveats.** Its authors said the analysis was unregistered, that seven offices can't establish a mechanism, and that a confirmatory test is registered for the follow-up.
- **The meetings evidence isn't only the correlation.** The treated–control difference in meeting time (3.8 v 7.1 hours) is a comparison between randomised groups, though one without pre-period data.
- **The standards are applied unevenly.** The comment dismisses an n = 7 correlation as unreplicable while promoting a two-point linear extrapolation of a survey measure as the explanation for the residual gain. A reader would reasonably expect the same caution in both places.

"Should not be cited as a mechanism" could fairly become "should be cited as a hypothesis pending Varden's registered confirmatory test." That is what Varden itself said.

## 6. Revenue doesn't belong among the problems behind the gain

The deflation is correct and worth reporting: the working paper's framing was misleading. But revenue plays no part in the per-hour calculation, so it can't "account for" any of the 23.4%. Present it separately.

CPI is also a rough deflator for firm revenue. Sector output-price indices, or comparison with sector revenue trends, would be better if available.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Sector §5:** the −11.2% for retail and hospitality comes from 3 organisations. The match with Varden's −11.4% is suggestive, but the n should be stated wherever the figure appears.
- **Time-tracking subset:** organisations that track time may differ systematically (more professional services, more billable work), which links to point 3. Give the sector mix of the 27, 23 and 17 subsets.
- **Unlogged work on the day off:** the comment notes this is probably not captured. That would make the corrected per-hour gain *smaller* still. Saying so is fine, but it reinforces the case for consistent hedging rather than "entirely."
- **The recommendations in §8 are sound:** record-based output, actual hours, comparison groups, follow-up of at least 18 months, and intention-to-treat analysis of all enrolled organisations.

## Overall

As a correction of the Halden working paper, the comment is largely convincing. The undisclosed post-start withdrawals, the manager-index overstatement and the scheduled-hours denominator are real and substantial. As a claim about reduced-hours schemes generally, it overreaches. The main revisions needed are:
- either actually correct for attrition or drop it from the "correcting the first three" claim;
- make the before-and-after comparison on the same subset;
- test novelty with the monthly output data;
- address Varden's case-processing result;
- describe Varden's meetings analysis accurately;
- replace "entirely an artifact" with a conclusion the corrected numbers support.

I can draft a revised abstract and conclusion, or a short reply-to-comment from the Halden authors' perspective.
